Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited Earnings Missed Analyst Estimates: Here's What Analysts Are Forecasting Now
sum: Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited (NSE:LLOYDSME) last week reported its latest second-quarter results, which makes it a good time for investors to dive in and see if the business is performing in line with expectations. It looks like a pretty bad result, all things considered. Although revenues of ₹57b were in line with analyst predictions, statutory earnings fell badly short, missing estimates by 31% to hit ₹18.38 per share. The analysts typically update their forecasts at each earnings report, and we can judge from their estimates whether their view of the company has changed or if there are any new concerns to be aware of. With this in mind, we've gathered the latest statutory forecasts to see what the analysts are expecting for next year.

Taking into account the latest results, the consensus forecast from Lloyds Metals and Energy's six analysts is for revenues of ₹298.2b in 2027. This reflects a major 24% improvement in revenue compared to the last 12 months. Statutory earnings per share are predicted to bounce 51% to ₹141. In the lead-up to this report, the analysts had been modelling revenues of ₹298.2b and earnings per share (EPS) of ₹141 in 2027. The consensus analysts don't seem to have seen anything in these results that would have changed their view on the business, given there's been no major change to their estimates.

With the analysts reconfirming their revenue and earnings forecasts, it's surprising to see that the price target rose 6.0% to ₹2,133. It looks as though they previously had some doubts over whether the business would live up to their expectations. Fixating on a single price target can be unwise though, since the consensus target is effectively the average of analyst price targets. As a result, some investors like to look at the range of estimates to see if there are any diverging opinions on the company's valuation. Currently, the most bullish analyst values Lloyds Metals and Energy at ₹2,389 per share, while the most bearish prices it at ₹1,879. This is a very narrow spread of estimates, implying either that Lloyds Metals and Energy is an easy company to value, or - more likely - the analysts are relying heavily on some key assumptions.

Lloyds shares at 94p! Time to sell?
sum: A fair few people got a fright in late October, including (probably) anyone taking a look at Lloyds' (LSE: LLOY) shares. The Halloween festivities coincided with the share price falling off a cliff on the back of a recent announcement by Chancellor John Healey of a windfall tax on banks. Lloyds' shares are now trading for pennies again – at 94p a pop, as I write.
Is a reversal of the 'banking surcharge' going to send shares in the Black Horse bank into a tailspin? Or is this simply market noise that's offering a chance to buy in cheap? Here's what I think.

Firstly, the much-predicted windfall tax was less impactful than it might have been. The basic detail is that the 'banking surcharge' has been temporarily increased for 15 months, taking it from 3% to 6%. The net effect is that banks like Lloyds will be losing 3% of earnings for just over a year.

A bigger impact in recent days was its 29 October earnings call. Shareholders might have been spooked by signs that things might be heading in the wrong direction. Net income increased 9% year on year, but there were worrying indications that margins are going to be squeezed. Net interest income's expected to be lower for 2027 on the back of competition in both lending and deposit markets. The share price dropped 6% on the day.

Eagle-eyed observers will however, note that the slide in Lloyds' shares – over 20%, meaning we are now firmly in crash territory – began all the way back in August. Not only that, but other FTSE 100 banks, and even ones abroad, are struggling too. So what the devil might be going on here?

One of the biggest issues for Lloyds is the short-term trajectory of the economy – in both the UK and the world at large. The success of banks is tied to the economies they operate in. More money flowing around means higher earnings.

So what's going on? Essentially, it's mostly down to the Iran war and its knock-on effects on inflation. Oil prices are loads higher than they were and shipping costs are on the up too. All this will have downstream effects on inflation.

sum: The diversified engineering and infrastructure company has now announced a fresh capital commitment to one of its newest subsidiaries. Structured in two stages and priced on an independent valuation, the move comes just as the group reports sharply higher half-year revenue, even as quarterly profit shows some signs of pressure.

The Nifty 50 traded at 23,684, up 1.06%, while the Sensex rose by 1.22% to 76,620 on Tuesday. Following this the Shares of LLOYDS ENGINEERING WORKS Ltd are trading at Rs. 79.82, down 5.86 percent on Tuesday. The stock touched the intraday high of Rs. 83.34 after opening at Rs. 81.55 before slipping to a low of Rs. 79.62. The company commands a market capitalization of Rs. 12,3570.90 crore.

SISCOL has become a meaningful part of the group since August 2026, when Lloyds lifted its stake to 51.70 percent. The subsidiary earned Rs 43.42 crore profit on Rs 816.87 crore turnover in FY26, and it brings an order book of Rs 1,260 crore. The fresh money should ease SISCOL’s liquidity and help it support heavy fabrication capacity, including its new Hyderabad facility.

There are points to watch. The standalone business used Rs 73.85 crore in operating cash flow during the half year, and the investment will draw on group resources. Because the companies share directors, investors will also watch the independent valuation and arm’s length pricing. Management says the transaction follows the Companies Act and SEBI rules.

Looking at the quarterly results of Lloyds Engineering Works Limited, the company’s consolidated revenue from operations increased by 87.44 percent YOY, from Rs. 316.66 crore in Q2 FY26 to Rs. 593.55 crore in Q2 FY27, and grew by 12.60 percent QoQ from Rs. 527.15 crore in Q1 FY27. For the half year, consolidated revenue rose 110 percent to Rs. 1,120.70 crore.

In Q2 FY27, consolidated net profit declined 0.46 percent YOY to Rs. 43.38 crore from Rs. 43.58 crore a year earlier. Against Q1 FY27, it fell 21.27 percent from Rs. 55.10 crore. Including its share of associate profit, net profit rose 6.29 percent YOY to Rs. 57.77 crore from Rs. 54.35 crore.
Basic earnings per share fell 7.32 percent to Rs. 0.38, compared with Rs. 0.41 in the same quarter of FY26.

sum: A Stocks and Shares ISA makes a brilliant home for dividend-paying UK shares. All shareholder payouts are tax-free, whether you reinvest them or draw them as income.

The good news is that plenty of FTSE 100 and FTSE 250 stocks offer attractive yields of 5%, 6% and in some cases more than 7%. With luck, that income should steadily rise as you reinvest dividends and companies increase payouts.
Nothing is guaranteed in investing, but I think these two FTSE 100 dividend stars are worth considering for an income portfolio today.
I’ve done brilliantly from wealth manager M&G (LSE: M&G). Its shares are up 20% over 12 months and 58% over five years, with dividends on top.

When I bought them, they yielded a stunning 10%. Such a dizzying yield can be a warning sign, but I believed it was sustainable. So far, I’ve been proved right. However, as the shares have climbed, the yield has slipped to 6.63% for new buyers. Still generous though. The board is also targeting annual dividend growth of around 2%. Although right now, that’s below inflation.
In the first half of 2026, M&G’s adjusted operating profit rose a solid 15% to £435m, driven by stronger asset-management revenues and growth in its life insurance business.

There are risks. A stock market crash could discourage customers from investing and reduce the commission-based fees M&G earns. It also operates in fiercely competitive markets, and is currently fighting a battle royale to win bulk annuity business from pension schemes. Passive tracker funds remain a constant challenge to its active management model.

sum: Compared to the start of 2026, Lloyds Banking Group (LSE:LLOY) shares are virtually unchanged.
However, those thinking about selling up might want to take a closer look at the latest analysts’ dividend predictions.
The consensus forecast is for the bank’s payout to increase significantly over the next four financial years:
If realised, this would be a remarkable outcome. It would lift the yield on the bank’s shares from 3.7% (using its 2025 payout) to 8.6%, when the 2030 forecast’s taken into account.
Based on dividends paid over the past 12 months, there’s no other stock on the FTSE 100 that currently (1 November) has a higher return than this.
Indeed, an 8%+ yield’s better than anything that could be earned on one of Lloyds’ savings accounts. It also beats the return available on gilts (government bonds).

However, it pays to be cautious. After all, dividends are never guaranteed. And there’s little point buying a stock for its income potential if its share price is likely to decline over the long term.

Lloyds Banking stock slips as Q3 profit jumps, targets hold
sum: Lloyds Banking Group reported stronger third-quarter profitability on Thursday, October 29, but kept its full-year targets unchanged. Lloyds Banking stock traded at 1.17 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 10:04 CET on Friday, October 30, 0.85 percent below the Xetra close of Thursday, October 29.

The bank's Q3 2026 results announcement, published on October 29, showed statutory profit before tax of 2.332 billion pounds for the three months to September 30, up 99 percent from 1.174 billion pounds a year earlier. The comparison benefited from the absence of the 875 million pound remediation charge recorded in the third quarter of 2025.

Net income rose 9 percent year on year to 5.072 billion pounds in the third quarter. Underlying net interest income reached 3.806 billion pounds, 10 percent above the prior-year quarter, while the banking net interest margin improved to 3.25 percent from 3.06 percent.

Lloyds said stronger structural hedge income and lending growth supported the quarter. Average interest-earning banking assets increased 1 percent from the second quarter to 481.0 billion pounds. The company also highlighted competitive conditions in the deposit market, which limited the pace of margin expansion and remains an important consideration for investors.

Underlying profit rose 83 percent year on year to 2.367 billion pounds. The quarterly return on tangible equity was 19.5 percent, compared with 7.5 percent a year earlier and 17.0 percent in the second quarter. The cost:income ratio improved to 47.2 percent from 68.4 percent in the prior-year quarter.

For the first nine months, statutory profit after tax increased 46 percent to 4.835 billion pounds, while earnings per share rose to 7.6 pence from 4.8 pence. Underlying profit increased 36 percent to 6.582 billion pounds. Net income rose 9 percent to 14.819 billion pounds, and underlying net interest income advanced 10 percent to 11.084 billion pounds.

Lloyds reiterated its 2026 targets. The group expects underlying net interest income above 14.9 billion pounds, a cost:income ratio below 50 percent, operating costs below 9.9 billion pounds, an asset quality ratio of about 25 basis points, return on tangible equity above 16 percent and capital generation above 200 basis points.

Lloyds Banking Group (NYSE: LYG) Beats Analyst Earnings Forecasts In Third Quarter Despite Stock Decline
sum: Lloyds Banking Group (NYSE: LYG) outpaced Wall Street’s earnings expectations in the third quarter, delivering results that edged past the consensus estimate tracked by Zacks Investment Research.
Three analysts surveyed by Zacks had forecast earnings of 14 cents per share, but the London-based bank came in a penny higher at 15 cents per share.
The earnings-per-share beat, while modest, signals that Lloyds continues to generate returns above what the market had priced in heading into the October 29 reporting date.
Total revenue for the quarter reached $7.34 billion, with revenue net of interest expense also recorded at $7.34 billion for the same period.

The bank’s headline quarterly profit came in at $2.15 billion, reflecting continued underlying strength across its core operations despite a challenging interest rate environment across British banking.
Lloyds, headquartered in London, remains one of the United Kingdom’s largest retail and commercial banking institutions, with its American depositary receipts trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Despite the earnings beat, shares fell sharply on the day results were published, declining 4.91%, a reaction that suggests investors may have been weighing broader macroeconomic concerns alongside the quarterly figures.

Lloyds, Barclays and NatWest shares jump as Healey softens bank tax blow
sum: UK bank shares rallied after Chancellor John Healey announced a smaller and shorter-lived tax increase on the sector than investors had feared.

Shares in Britain’s biggest banks jumped on Wednesday after Chancellor John Healey unveiled a more limited tax increase on the sector than investors had expected, easing concerns that lenders would face a prolonged squeeze on profits.
Lloyds Banking Group shares rose 4.2%, while Barclays gained 3.7% and NatWest climbed 2.4% following the announcement.

The gains suggest investors were relieved that the government had stopped short of imposing a larger and more permanent tax burden on banks, which have benefited from higher interest rates in recent years.
The banking sector had been braced for additional taxation as Healey sought to raise revenue while balancing pressure to support economic growth and maintain confidence in the public finances.
But the Chancellor’s decision to limit both the scale and duration of the increase helped ease some of those concerns, triggering a rally in UK banking stocks.

The share price moves underline how closely investors have been watching the government’s approach to taxing financial institutions, particularly as lenders face pressure to maintain profitability while supporting households and businesses.

items.t: 28 October: a big day for Lloyds shares?
sum: What’s going on with Lloyds‘ (LSE: LLOY) shares? The share price seems to be on a bit of a downward swing at the moment. A high of 117p earlier in the year has eased back to 103p on 7 October.

One possible reason for the retreat is a few nerves around the upcoming fiddling with the government’s finances. Following Prime Minister’s Questions on 28 October, Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Autumn Budget – and Lloyds could be squarely in the crosshairs…

The rumours are that a windfall tax on the banking sector is going to be introduced. The justification is that banks are going through something of a purple patch on the back of elevated interest rates – higher borrowing costs tend to widen margins. In Lloyds’ case, we can see a dividend that has doubled since 2021.
Is a windfall tax likely? The latest rumours suggest it. Apparently, Healey has warned bosses of Britain’s biggest banks the government is in a “difficult fiscal position”.

The government needs the money to keep the fiscal headroom intact. That was a key manifesto promise. Another one of the promises made prior to the 2024 election was not to touch taxes on working people like income tax or VAT.

That leaves few places to extract dough for the government coffers. The clincher might be that banks are seen as fair game in this respect. For better or worse, few voters will go into mourning because of a tax on banks.

What will the impact be? This depends largely on the nature of any tax. A one-off raid is unlikely to make too much of a dent in the share price. A big and permanent levy on banking profits could do lasting damage to the sector.

Is there any value left in Lloyds shares at £1.07?
sum: Lloyds' (LSE: LLOY) shares are up 29% over the year and 133% over five years. This begs the natural question of whether any value can be left in the stock now?
Factoring in strong earnings growth potential, relative undervaluation to its peers, and absolute undervaluation to projected profits, I think there is. And it could be a lot.
So how much exactly are we looking at here over the short- and long-term?
The 19 major analysts covering Lloyds have a consensus short-term (one-year) price target of £1.21. That represents a 13.1% increase on the current price of £1.07.
One key positive underlying this is the bank's ability to reinvest short-term customer deposits into longer-term, higher-yielding assets.

Another positive factor is Lloyds' track record of setting conservative financial targets and then outperforming them. Analysts' price forecasts are based on official figures from companies, and if these are exceeded, then price targets are raised.
And the final positive element is the bank's aggressive share buyback strategy. This reduces the supply of shares in the market, which — if demand remains steady — will boost the price.

Lloyds Banking Group Shares Eye 52-Week High as Bullish Momentum Builds
sum: Shares in Lloyds Banking Group (LON: LLOY) are on course to close near their 52-week high, extending a powerful rally that has seen the stock climb roughly 52% over the past year.
Despite a 0.4% decline on Tuesday, the FTSE 100 lender was last trading around 114.9p, just above its recent intraday peak of 116p struck on Monday.

From a technical standpoint, the setup remains constructive. Lloyds has been carving out a clear series of higher highs and higher lows since bottoming near 73.5p last summer, with the stock accelerating sharply through the second quarter of 2026.

The breakout above the 110p resistance zone in late June proved pivotal, flipping what had been a psychological ceiling into fresh support. Since then, price action has consolidated in a tight range between 111p and 116p, a pattern often associated with continuation rather than exhaustion.

Volume has been notably heavy on up-days, particularly around the 111p-115p breakout zone, suggesting institutional accumulation rather than speculative froth. The 50-day moving average continues to slope upward and sits well below current price, offering a dynamic support level should momentum stall. Meanwhile, the stock’s proximity to 52-week highs — often a bullish signal in momentum-based strategies — has attracted renewed attention from technical traders.

That said, a slight pullback of around 0.7% in the latest session, alongside chatter about the Bank of England’s capital framework and Lloyds’ ongoing buyback programme, hints the stock may need to digest recent gains before any decisive push through 116p. A confirmed close above that level on strong volume would likely open the door toward fresh all-time highs not seen since the financial crisis era, while failure to hold above 110p could signal near-term exhaustion.
For now, the broader trend remains firmly bullish, and Lloyds looks set to notch another milestone close near its yearly high.
